history: Cleopatra VII ruled Egypt from 51 to 30 BC, and almost nothing people picture about her is Egyptian. Her family, the Ptolemies, were Macedonian Greeks who had held the throne for roughly three centuries and mostly never bothered to learn the local language. Cleopatra did, and was reportedly fluent in a string of others besides.

She also sits oddly in time. The Great Pyramid of Giza was already about two and a half thousand years old when she was born — meaning she lived closer to the invention of the pizza and the Moon landing than to the building of the pyramid she would have seen from her own kingdom.

Napoleon Bonaparte was not short. He stood somewhere around 5 foot 6 or 7 in modern measurements, which was unremarkable for a Frenchman of his day. The myth comes partly from French inches being longer than English ones, and mostly from British caricaturists who found a tiny ranting emperor funnier than an average-sized one.

1805 was his best year and his worst. In October the Royal Navy destroyed the combined French and Spanish fleets at Trafalgar, ending any hope of invading Britain. Six weeks later he won at Austerlitz, generally considered his finest battle, by deliberately weakening his own right flank to bait an attack.

The beaked plague mask is the most recognisable image of the Black Death, and it is roughly 270 years too late for it. The 1348 outbreak had no such thing. The beak was described in 1619 by Charles de Lorme, physician to the French court, and belongs to the plague waves of the 1600s.

The theory behind it was miasma: that disease travelled in foul air. The beak was packed with herbs and spices to filter what doctors breathed. It did nothing for a bacterium carried by fleas, but the waxed coat and gloves may have offered some accidental protection by keeping the fleas off.

In 1932 Australia declared war on birds and lost. Around 20,000 emus had moved into Western Australian farmland, and the government despatched soldiers of the Royal Australian Artillery under Major G. P. W. Meredith with two Lewis machine guns.

The emus scattered into small groups, ran at speeds the gunners could not track, and absorbed hits without going down. After roughly a week the operation was withdrawn, restarted, and abandoned again. Meredith later remarked that if he had a division with the birds' ability to take bullets, it would face any army in the world.

In July 1518 a woman recorded as Frau Troffea stepped into a street in Strasbourg and began to dance. She did not stop. Within a week dozens had joined her, within a month several hundred, and contemporary accounts describe people dancing until they collapsed.

The authorities concluded the cure was more dancing, cleared guildhalls and hired musicians to keep the afflicted moving. It made things worse. Historians still argue over the cause — mass psychogenic illness brought on by famine and disease is the leading explanation; ergot poisoning from mouldy rye is the popular one, though it struggles to explain sustained coordinated movement.

Grigori Rasputin was murdered in St Petersburg in December 1916 by a group of nobles who believed his hold over the Tsarina was destroying Russia. The story everyone knows — poisoned cakes and wine that did nothing, several bullets, a beating, and finally drowning — comes largely from the memoirs of one of his killers, Felix Yusupov, who had a book to sell.

The autopsy was less theatrical and more grim: a gunshot to the head, and no evidence of poison in his system. He was dead before he reached the water. The legend of the man who would not die was manufactured almost immediately, and has comfortably outlived the facts.

Dutch tulip mania peaked in the winter of 1636 and collapsed in February 1637. At the height, contracts for a single rare bulb changed hands for sums comparable to an Amsterdam house. The most prized were not solid colours but flamed and feathered ones — an effect, nobody then knew, produced by a virus infecting the bulb.

The popular version has ruined merchants hurling themselves into canals. Recent work by historians such as Anne Goldgar found little evidence of that. Most trades were paper contracts among a fairly small circle, few were ever settled, and the lasting damage was to trust and reputation rather than to the Dutch economy.

In 1717 Edward Teach captured a French slave ship called La Concorde, renamed her Queen Anne's Revenge, and fitted her with around forty guns. Within a year Blackbeard was the most feared name in the Atlantic, and he achieved it with remarkably little killing.

His weapon was theatre. He braided slow-burning fuses into his beard and hair and lit them before boarding, so he appeared through his own smoke. Terrified crews surrendered without a fight, which was the entire point: a surrendered ship is worth far more than a damaged one.

In 79 AD Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under volcanic ash and surge deposits. The ash is also why we know so much about ordinary Roman life — it sealed bread still in ovens, election notices on walls, and a great deal of graffiti that makes clear Romans were exactly as crude as everyone else.

The Roman army of the period was less a horde than a logistics operation. A legionary marched carrying armour, weapons, tools, cooking equipment and rations, and was expected to help build a fortified camp at the end of the day's march. The fighting was the easy part.

By 870 the Norse were settling Iceland, raiding across the Irish Sea and trading as far as Byzantium. The horned helmet is an invention of the 1800s, largely down to costume design for Wagner's operas; no Viking-age horned helmet has ever been excavated.

They were also unusually clean for the period. Combs, tweezers and ear spoons turn up constantly in Norse graves, and an English chronicler grumbled that the Danes combed their hair daily, bathed on Saturdays and changed their clothes often — and thereby had unfair success with English women.

By 1640 Japan had effectively closed itself. A series of edicts under the Tokugawa shogunate barred most foreigners, banned Japanese subjects from leaving, and made returning home a capital offence. Dutch traders were confined to Dejima, a fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbour, which stayed Japan's narrow window on the outside world for over two centuries.

The samurai of this era had a problem: peace. With no wars to fight, a warrior class was gradually reduced to administrators and bureaucrats, drawing salaries in rice and increasingly in debt to the merchants they officially outranked.

On 28 December 1895 the Lumière brothers held the first commercial film screening in a Paris basement. The famous story that audiences fled a train arriving at La Ciotat is almost certainly a later embellishment.

The same Paris had the Moulin Rouge, open since 1889, where the can-can was performed and Toulouse-Lautrec drank, drew, and made the posters that would outlive the dancers. Belle Epoque Paris was simultaneously the most glamorous and the most tubercular city in Europe.

The German witch trials of the 1600s were among the deadliest in Europe. In the prince-bishoprics of Würzburg and Bamberg alone, several hundred people were executed within a few years. Most were women, most were poor, and confessions were extracted under torture that no account can honestly separate from the words produced.

The trials fed on themselves: a confession required naming accomplices, which produced more accusations, which produced more trials. They ended not because anyone was found innocent, but because the machinery eventually reached people powerful enough to stop it.

Venice in 1610 was a republic run on secrecy. The Council of Ten operated an intelligence network across Europe, and citizens could post anonymous denunciations into stone letterboxes — the bocche di leone, lion's mouths — set into walls around the city.

It was also the year Galileo published Sidereus Nuncius in Venice, reporting the moons of Jupiter and a Moon with mountains on it. The Venetian Senate had already given him a pay rise for the telescope, having grasped immediately what it was worth to a maritime power that wanted to see ships before the ships saw them.

Chicago in 1927 was Al Capone's city, and Prohibition had done the opposite of what was intended. Banning the legal liquor trade handed an enormous untaxed market to anyone willing to break the law, and the profits bought police, judges and elections.

Capone was never convicted of anything to do with the violence. In 1931 the federal government got him on tax evasion — the logic being that income is taxable whether or not you earned it legally. He served most of his sentence at Alcatraz.

Victorian London's great engineering achievement was not a railway but a sewer. After the Great Stink of 1858 made Parliament itself unusable, Joseph Bazalgette was authorised to build some 1,100 miles of sewers beneath the city.

He sized the pipes for the largest population he could imagine, then doubled the diameter, reasoning that this was the sort of thing one only gets to do once. That decision kept the system working for over a century longer than it had any right to.

The Normandy landings of 6 June 1944 put roughly 156,000 Allied troops ashore in a single day, supported by a deception operation that convinced German command the real invasion was coming at Calais — a belief some held for weeks afterwards.

The war also produced Lieutenant Colonel Jack Churchill, a real British officer who carried a longbow, a broadsword and a set of bagpipes into the Second World War, and is credited with the last recorded longbow kill in British military history. His stated view was that any officer going into action without his sword was improperly dressed.

London punk in 1977 lasted about eighteen months and rearranged British music permanently. The Roxy in Covent Garden ran as a punk venue for roughly a hundred days; the Sex Pistols released Never Mind the Bollocks in October, and shops were prosecuted for displaying the title.

The scene's actual innovation was not the noise but the premise: that you could form a band before you could play. A famous fanzine printed three chord diagrams and the instruction to go and form a band. Most of what followed in British independent music came out of people taking that literally.

The Batcave opened in Soho in July 1982 and gave the emerging goth scene a home and, eventually, a name it mostly disliked. The music press coined 'gothic' as a description; the bands spent years objecting to it.

The aesthetic drew on Victorian mourning dress, Hammer horror and German expressionist cinema — and on a genuine Victorian industry. Nineteenth-century Britain had strict mourning etiquette and shops devoted entirely to black crape, jet jewellery and the correct clothing for each stage of grief.

The 1980s fitness boom was built on home video. Jane Fonda's Workout, released in 1982, became one of the best-selling home videos of the decade and helped sell VCRs to households that had no other reason to own one.

The look — leotard over tights, leg warmers, headband — came out of dance rehearsal wear, routed through the film Flashdance in 1983. Leg warmers have a real purpose for dancers, keeping muscles warm between takes. Almost nobody wearing them to aerobics class in 1984 needed them.

The North American video game crash of 1983 nearly killed the industry. The market was flooded with poor titles on the Atari 2600, retailers lost confidence, and revenues collapsed by something like 97 per cent over two years.

The emblem of it was a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico, where Atari buried truckloads of unsold cartridges, including the notoriously rushed E.T. game. It was treated as an urban legend for thirty years until a 2014 excavation dug the cartridges up and proved it true.

The 1983 toy aisle ran on a rule change. Until 1984 US regulators effectively banned programme-length commercials for children, which kept cartoons and toy lines apart. When the restriction was relaxed, a cartoon could exist purely to sell the figures.

He-Man had arrived in 1982 with the logic reversed: the toys came first, and the fiction was written afterwards to explain them. The figures sold in enormous numbers, and nearly every action-figure cartoon of the decade followed the same order of operations.

Flash Gordon reached cinemas as a serial in 1936, with Buster Crabbe in the lead and a budget large enough to make it the most expensive serial of its day. Audiences watched a chapter a week, each one ending on a cliffhanger engineered to sell next week's ticket.

Those cliffhangers were frequently cheated. A hero shown plunging to certain death would be revealed the following week to have jumped clear a moment earlier — in footage that had not been in the previous instalment at all. The serial format, and that specific trick, shaped the blockbusters that came decades later.

The 1980s action film ran on a small, repeatable formula: an outnumbered hero, a jungle or a tower block, an armoury of implausible weapons, and a one-liner delivered over the corpse. The genre was enormously profitable and almost entirely interchangeable.

The weapons were mostly cinematic fiction. The shoulder-fired miniguns of the era weigh far too much to carry, let alone fire by hand, and need an external power source. Blank-firing props and hidden mounts did the work the biceps got the credit for.

Sunset Strip in 1987 was the centre of glam metal. Bands flyered the Strip by hand, played the Whisky and the Roxy, and were signed on the strength of a crowd rather than a demo. Appetite for Destruction came out that year and went on to become one of the best-selling debut albums ever made.

The hair required industrial quantities of aerosol spray, and the scene ended almost overnight. When Nevermind arrived in 1991, labels dropped glam acts within months. Few genres have been replaced that fast.

Lucha libre in 1955 was in its golden age, and its central rule is the mask. A luchador's mask is treated as an identity rather than a costume, and the highest stake in the sport is the mask-versus-mask match, where the loser is unmasked publicly and permanently.
El Santo wore his for nearly fifty years, in the ring, in films and in public, and was buried in it. He removed it on television only once, a week before his death.
The axolotl itself is Mexican, native to the lake system beneath Mexico City. It can regrow limbs, parts of its heart and portions of its brain, and it is critically endangered in the wild.

The future as imagined in 1953 was all rockets and rayguns and almost no computers. Fins, bubble helmets, and a crew who navigated by eye — because the idea that a machine might do the arithmetic had not yet taken hold in popular fiction.

Real 1953 was a strange year to guess from. The structure of DNA was published that April, and the first ascent of Everest was reported in London on the morning of the coronation. Space travel was still four years from Sputnik.

The last Ice Age ended around 11,700 years ago, and for much of it Europe was steppe and tundra rather than forest. Sea levels were low enough that Britain was joined to the continent by a landmass archaeologists call Doggerland, now under the North Sea, where trawlers still occasionally bring up tools and bone.

Ice Age people were not merely surviving. The cave paintings at Chauvet and Lascaux, the carved figurines, the bone flutes — the oldest known instruments are over 40,000 years old. Art is roughly as old as we are.

The 'Florida Man' phenomenon is a quirk of public records law rather than of Florida. The state's Sunshine Law is unusually broad, making arrest reports and mugshots easily available to any reporter who asks.

Journalists in other states frequently cannot get the same material, so the same sort of story simply never gets written. Florida does not produce stranger events than anywhere else. It produces better documentation of them.

The 2021 crypto cycle ran on a vocabulary invented almost by accident. 'HODL' began as a drunk misspelling of 'hold' in a 2013 forum post by someone explaining why he was not selling, and was retroactively turned into an acronym by people who found the original story insufficiently dignified.

The cycle peaked in November 2021 and fell roughly 75 per cent over the following year. The pattern — a new asset, a wave of certainty, a long retreat — is old enough that the Dutch tulip traders of 1637 would have recognised the shape of it.
The open-plan office was invented to make work more human. The German Bürolandschaft movement of the 1950s proposed scattered, plant-screened desks as an escape from regimented rows.

What crossed the Atlantic was the cheap part. Robert Propst designed the Action Office in 1968 as flexible, height-variable workspace; employers bought the panels, packed them tight and produced the cubicle. Propst spent the rest of his life saying he had not intended that, and called the result monolithic insanity.

Greyhounds are the fastest dogs alive, capable of around 45 miles per hour, and they sleep roughly eighteen hours a day. They are sprinters, not distance runners: enormous acceleration, a very short tank, and an overwhelming preference for the sofa.

Their build is ancient. Dogs of recognisably greyhound shape appear in Egyptian tomb art thousands of years old, which makes the modern racing dog one of the oldest continuously recognisable animal silhouettes in human art.

The golden retriever was created in the Scottish Highlands in the second half of the 1800s by Dudley Marjoribanks, Lord Tweedmouth, who kept meticulous stud books. Every golden retriever alive descends from that programme.

They were bred to carry shot game back undamaged, which required a dog with a soft mouth and an unusual willingness to hand things over. The retrieving instinct that makes them tireless about a thrown ball is the same trait, with nothing left to retrieve.
Flamingos are not born pink. They hatch grey and turn pink from carotenoid pigments in the algae and brine shrimp they eat, filtered through a beak held upside down in the water.

Miami's other pink is Art Deco. The South Beach district holds one of the largest concentrations of 1930s Deco architecture anywhere, saved from demolition in the 1970s and 80s by a preservation campaign led largely by Barbara Baer Capitman. The famous pastel paint scheme was applied later, by a designer, and is not original.

Bondi's surf lifesaving club, founded in 1907, is among the oldest in the world, and the reel, line and belt rescue method developed in Australia saved an enormous number of lives before powered craft.

Kangaroos cannot walk backwards in any practical sense — the tail and the shape of the hind legs make it close to impossible. This is the stated reason a kangaroo appears on the Australian coat of arms: an animal that only goes forward.

Golden Age Hollywood ran on contracts that would now be illegal. Studios signed actors for seven years, chose their films, changed their names, arranged their marriages for publicity, and suspended anyone who refused a role — adding the suspension to the end of the contract.

Olivia de Havilland sued Warner Bros. over exactly that practice and won in 1944. The ruling, still known in California as the de Havilland Law, capped personal service contracts at seven calendar years and broke the studio system's grip on its own stars.

The office cubicle was meant to set workers free. Robert Propst designed the Action Office for Herman Miller in the 1960s as a flexible, open workspace. Companies took the cheap part of the idea, the partitions, and packed people in. Propst spent his later years calling the result 'monolithic insanity'.

Capybaras, meanwhile, became famous for being unbothered. In 1982 a keeper at Izu Shaboten Zoo in Japan noticed them crowding into a puddle of warm water, and the zoo has given them a hot spring bath every winter since.

Around the year 890 a Norwegian chieftain named Ohthere visited King Alfred in England and described his home in the far north. Alfred's scribes wrote it down. Ohthere said he had sailed north partly for the walruses, 'because they have very fine ivory in their tusks', and he brought some as a gift.

The cod he would have fished are still caught off Lofoten every winter. Hung on wooden racks, the fish dries in the cold wind into stockfish, which keeps for years. It was one of the first things Norway ever exported.

In August 1609 Galileo carried his new telescope up the bell tower in St Mark's Square and let the senators of Venice look through it. They could see ships two hours before they reached port, and they doubled his salary. The next March he published what he had seen in the sky, in Venice.

Venice was also where a painter went shopping. The city had specialist colour-sellers, the vendecolori, who dealt in pigments from all over the trading world, including ultramarine ground from lapis lazuli that cost more than gold.

Late in 1932 the Australian army sent soldiers with two Lewis machine guns into the wheat country of Western Australia to deal with some twenty thousand emus that were eating the crops. The birds scattered, ran, and soaked up bullets. After about a month and ten thousand rounds the army went home. The emus stayed.

The same state was built on gold. Paddy Hannan's find near Kalgoorlie in 1893 started a rush, and in 1931 a seventeen-year-old named Jim Larcombe dug up the Golden Eagle, a nugget weighing more than 1,100 ounces, the largest ever found in Western Australia.

Sherlock Holmes first appeared in print in 1887, in A Study in Scarlet. The famous deerstalker hat is never named in any of the stories. It came from the illustrator, Sidney Paget, who drew Holmes in one for The Strand Magazine, and the picture stuck harder than the text.

Real detectives of the 1880s had far less to work with. Scotland Yard did not open its Fingerprint Bureau until 1901. Before that, identifying a repeat offender meant measuring the lengths of his head, arms and feet and looking him up in a card index.

Prohibition made undercover work a career. The most famous agents were Izzy Einstein and Moe Smith in New York, who got into speakeasies disguised as gravediggers, opera singers and football players, and made 4,932 arrests between them before the Bureau let them go in 1925 for being more famous than their bosses.

Chicago in 1927 was Al Capone's town, and there were thousands of places to get a drink. The law that banned alcohol never banned drinking it, only making, moving and selling it, which is one reason so few people felt like criminals.

On the night of 31 May 1942 three Japanese midget submarines slipped into Sydney Harbour. One torpedo missed an American cruiser and sank a converted ferry, killing twenty-one sailors. A week later a submarine surfaced offshore and shelled the eastern suburbs, around Rose Bay and Bondi.

For the rest of the war Bondi Beach was strung with barbed wire and tank traps against an invasion that never came. Sydney filled with servicemen on leave, and the dance halls and canteens stayed open late to keep up with them.
The Colosseum opened in 80 AD under the emperor Titus, with a hundred days of games. It could seat around fifty thousand people and had a canvas awning, worked by sailors, to keep the sun off them.

Gladiators were the celebrities of their day. Graffiti scratched on a wall in Pompeii calls a fighter named Celadus 'the sigh of the girls', and another, Crescens, 'lord of the maidens'. Most gladiators were slaves, and the famous ones were worth far too much to waste, so many fights ended with both men walking out.

In the 1780s an Italian doctor, Luigi Galvani, found that a dead frog's leg kicked when he touched it with two different metals. He published in 1791 and called it 'animal electricity'. His nephew took the idea on tour, wiring up the bodies of executed criminals in front of paying crowds.

A teenager named Mary Shelley grew up hearing about those shows. In 1818 she published Frankenstein. The book never says exactly how the creature is brought to life; the lightning and the laboratory came later, from the stage and the films.

Venice guarded its secrets like treasure. From 1291 the city's glassmakers were made to live and work on the island of Murano, partly for fear of fire and partly so nobody could carry the craft abroad. A master who left the Republic without permission could be hunted down.

The city also ran on anonymous tips. Stone letterboxes carved as open mouths, the bocche di leone, were set into the walls of public buildings so that citizens could post accusations against their neighbours. Some are still there in the Doge's Palace.

At the 1939 World's Fair in New York, Westinghouse showed off Elektro, a seven-foot aluminium man who could walk on command, speak about seven hundred recorded words, count on his fingers and smoke a cigarette. He later got a robot dog called Sparko.

The first robot with a real job was far less charming. Unimate, a one-armed machine, started work at a General Motors plant in New Jersey in 1961, lifting hot metal castings off a line so that people no longer had to.

Tutankhamun became pharaoh at about eight or nine and died at about eighteen or nineteen, around 1323 BC. He was a minor king, and that is why he is famous: his small tomb was overlooked by robbers, and Howard Carter found it nearly intact in 1922.

Among the thousands of objects inside was a dagger with an iron blade, made centuries before Egyptians could smelt iron. In 2016 tests confirmed that the metal came from a meteorite. The Egyptians had a phrase for the material: 'iron from the sky'.

The bald eagle has been on the Great Seal of the United States since 1782. Benjamin Franklin was not a fan. In a letter to his daughter two years later he called it 'a bird of bad moral character' that steals fish from other birds, and said the turkey was 'a much more respectable bird'. He never proposed the turkey officially.

The longest inaugural address belongs to William Henry Harrison, who in 1841 spoke for nearly two hours in the cold, about 8,400 words. He died a month later, the shortest presidency in American history.

The phrase 'flying saucer' dates from June 1947, when a pilot named Kenneth Arnold reported nine shining objects near Mount Rainier and said they moved like a saucer skipped across water. Newspapers did the rest.

Two weeks later the army air base at Roswell, New Mexico, announced that it had recovered a 'flying disc' from a ranch, then said the next day that it was a weather balloon. In 1994 the Air Force gave a third answer: the wreckage came from Project Mogul, a secret programme of high-altitude balloons built to listen for Soviet nuclear tests.
